{{Short description|Concept in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], a [[line bundle]] on a [[projective variety]] is '''nef''' if it has nonnegative degree on every [[algebraic curve|curve]] in the variety. The classes of nef line bundles are described by a [[convex cone]], and the possible contractions of the variety correspond to certain faces of the nef cone. In view of the correspondence between line bundles and [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisors]] (built from [[codimension]]-1 subvarieties), there is an equivalent notion of a '''nef divisor'''.

==Definition==
More generally, a line bundle ''L'' on a [[proper morphism|proper]] [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''X'' over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''k'' is said to be '''nef''' if it has nonnegative degree on every (closed [[irreducible component|irreducible]]) curve in ''X''.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Definition 1.4.1.</ref> (The '''[[divisor (algebraic geometry)#Divisor class group|degree]]''' of a line bundle ''L'' on a proper curve ''C'' over ''k'' is the degree of the divisor (''s'') of any nonzero rational section ''s'' of ''L''.) A line bundle may also be called an [[invertible sheaf]].

The term "nef" was introduced by [[Miles Reid]] as a replacement for the older terms "arithmetically effective" {{harv|Zariski|1962|loc=definition 7.6}} and "numerically effective", as well as for the phrase "numerically eventually free".<ref>Reid (1983), section 0.12f.</ref> The older terms were misleading, in view of the examples [[#Examples|below]].

Every line bundle ''L'' on a proper curve ''C'' over ''k'' which has a [[global section]] that is not identically zero has nonnegative degree. As a result, a [[basepoint-free]] line bundle on a proper scheme ''X'' over ''k'' has nonnegative degree on every curve in ''X''; that is, it is nef.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 1.4.5.</ref> More generally, a line bundle ''L'' is called '''semi-ample''' if some positive [[tensor product of line bundles|tensor power]] <math>L^{\otimes a}</math> is basepoint-free. It follows that a semi-ample line bundle is nef. Semi-ample line bundles can be considered the main geometric source of nef line bundles, although the two concepts are not equivalent; see the examples [[#Examples|below]].

A [[Cartier divisor]] ''D'' on a proper scheme ''X'' over a field is said to be nef if the [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|associated line bundle]] ''O''(''D'') is nef on ''X''. Equivalently, ''D'' is nef if the [[intersection number]] <math>D\cdot C</math> is nonnegative for every curve ''C'' in ''X''.

To go back from line bundles to divisors, the '''first Chern class''' is the isomorphism from the [[Picard group]] of line bundles on a variety ''X'' to the group of Cartier divisors modulo [[linear equivalence]]. Explicitly, the first Chern class <math>c_1(L)</math> is the divisor (''s'') of any nonzero rational section ''s'' of ''L''.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 1.1.5.</ref>

==The nef cone==
To work with inequalities, it is convenient to consider '''R'''-divisors, meaning finite [[linear combination]]s of Cartier divisors with [[real number|real]] coefficients. The '''R'''-divisors modulo [[Adequate equivalence relation|numerical equivalence]] form a real [[vector space]] <math>N^1(X)</math> of finite dimension, the [[Néron–Severi group]] [[tensor product of modules|tensored]] with the real numbers.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 1.3.10.</ref> (Explicitly: two '''R'''-divisors are said to be numerically equivalent if they have the same intersection number with all curves in ''X''.) An '''R'''-divisor is called nef if it has nonnegative degree on every curve. The nef '''R'''-divisors form a closed convex cone in <math>N^1(X)</math>, the '''nef cone''' Nef(''X'').

The '''[[cone of curves]]''' is defined to be the convex cone of linear combinations of curves with nonnegative real coefficients in the real vector space <math>N_1(X)</math> of 1-cycles modulo numerical equivalence. The vector spaces <math>N^1(X)</math> and <math>N_1(X)</math> are [[dual space|dual]] to each other by the intersection pairing, and the nef cone is (by definition) the [[dual cone]] of the cone of curves.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Definition 1.4.25.</ref>

A significant problem in algebraic geometry is to analyze which line bundles are [[ample line bundle|ample]], since that amounts to describing the different ways a variety can be embedded into projective space. One answer is '''Kleiman's criterion''' (1966): for a projective scheme ''X'' over a field, a line bundle (or '''R'''-divisor) is ample if and only if its class in <math>N^1(X)</math> lies in the interior of the nef cone.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Theorem 1.4.23.</ref> (An '''R'''-divisor is called ample if it can be written as a positive linear combination of ample Cartier divisors.) It follows from Kleiman's criterion that, for ''X'' projective, every nef '''R'''-divisor on ''X'' is a limit of ample '''R'''-divisors in <math>N^1(X)</math>. Indeed, for ''D'' nef and ''A'' ample, ''D'' + ''cA'' is ample for all real numbers ''c'' > 0.

==Metric definition of nef line bundles==
Let ''X'' be a [[compact complex manifold]] with a fixed [[Hermitian metric]], viewed as a positive [[complex differential form|(1,1)-form]] <math>\omega</math>. Following [[Jean-Pierre Demailly]], Thomas Peternell and Michael Schneider, a [[holomorphic line bundle]] ''L'' on ''X'' is said to be '''nef''' if for every <math>\epsilon > 0</math> there is a [[smoothness|smooth]] Hermitian metric <math>h_\epsilon</math> on ''L'' whose [[Hermitian vector bundle|curvature]] satisfies
<math>\Theta_{h_\epsilon}(L)\geq -\epsilon\omega</math>.
When ''X'' is projective over '''C''', this is equivalent to the previous definition (that ''L'' has nonnegative degree on all curves in ''X'').<ref>Demailly et al. (1994), section 1.</ref>

Even for ''X'' projective over '''C''', a nef line bundle ''L'' need not have a Hermitian metric ''h'' with curvature <math>\Theta_h(L)\geq 0</math>, which explains the more complicated definition just given.<ref>Demailly et al. (1994), Example 1.7.</ref>

==Examples==
*If ''X'' is a smooth projective surface and ''C'' is an (irreducible) curve in ''X'' with self-intersection number <math>C^2\geq 0</math>, then ''C'' is nef on ''X'', because any two ''distinct'' curves on a surface have nonnegative intersection number. If <math>C^2<0</math>, then ''C'' is effective but not nef on ''X''. For example, if ''X'' is the [[blowing up|blow-up]] of a smooth projective surface ''Y'' at a point, then the exceptional curve ''E'' of the blow-up <math>\pi\colon X\to Y</math> has <math>E^2=-1</math>.
*Every effective divisor on a [[flag manifold]] or [[abelian variety]] is nef, using that these varieties have a [[transitive action]] of a connected [[algebraic group]].<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 1.4.7.</ref>
*Every line bundle ''L'' of degree 0 on a smooth complex projective curve ''X'' is nef, but ''L'' is semi-ample if and only if ''L'' is [[torsion (algebra)|torsion]] in the Picard group of ''X''. For ''X'' of [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] ''g'' at least 1, most line bundles of degree 0 are not torsion, using that the [[Jacobian variety|Jacobian]] of ''X'' is an abelian variety of dimension ''g''.
*Every semi-ample line bundle is nef, but not every nef line bundle is even numerically equivalent to a semi-ample line bundle. For example, [[David Mumford]] constructed a line bundle ''L'' on a suitable [[ruled surface#Ruled surfaces in algebraic geometry|ruled surface]] ''X'' such that ''L'' has positive degree on all curves, but the intersection number <math>c_1(L)^2</math> is zero.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 1.5.2.</ref> It follows that ''L'' is nef, but no positive multiple of <math>c_1(L)</math> is numerically equivalent to an effective divisor. In particular, the space of global sections <math>H^0(X,L^{\otimes a})</math> is zero for all positive integers ''a''.

==Contractions and the nef cone==
A '''[[contraction morphism|contraction]]''' of a [[normal scheme|normal]] projective variety ''X'' over a field ''k'' is a surjective morphism <math>f\colon X\to Y</math> with ''Y'' a normal projective variety over ''k'' such that <math>f_*\mathcal{O}_X=\mathcal{O}_Y</math>. (The latter condition implies that ''f'' has [[connected space|connected]] fibers, and it is equivalent to ''f'' having connected fibers if ''k'' has [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Definition 2.1.11.</ref>) A contraction is called a '''fibration''' if dim(''Y'') < dim(''X''). A contraction with dim(''Y'') = dim(''X'') is automatically a [[birational morphism]].<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Example 2.1.12.</ref> (For example, ''X'' could be the blow-up of a smooth projective surface ''Y'' at a point.)

A '''face''' ''F'' of a convex cone ''N'' means a convex subcone such that any two points of ''N'' whose sum is in ''F'' must themselves be in ''F''. A contraction of ''X'' determines a face ''F'' of the nef cone of ''X'', namely the intersection of Nef(''X'') with the [[pullback bundle|pullback]] <math>f^*(N^1(Y))\subset N^1(X)</math>. Conversely, given the variety ''X'', the face ''F'' of the nef cone determines the contraction <math>f\colon X\to Y</math> up to isomorphism. Indeed, there is a semi-ample line bundle ''L'' on ''X'' whose class in <math>N^1(X)</math> is in the interior of ''F'' (for example, take ''L'' to be the pullback to ''X'' of any ample line bundle on ''Y''). Any such line bundle determines ''Y'' by the [[Proj construction]]:<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Theorem 2.1.27.</ref>
:<math>Y=\text{Proj }\bigoplus_{a\geq 0}H^0(X,L^{\otimes a}).</math>
To describe ''Y'' in geometric terms: a curve ''C'' in ''X'' maps to a point in ''Y'' if and only if ''L'' has degree zero on ''C''.

As a result, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the contractions of ''X'' and some of the faces of the nef cone of ''X''.<ref>Kollár & Mori (1998), Remark 1.26.</ref> (This correspondence can also be formulated dually, in terms of faces of the cone of curves.) Knowing which nef line bundles are semi-ample would determine which faces correspond to contractions. The [[cone theorem]] describes a significant class of faces that do correspond to contractions, and the [[abundance conjecture]] would give more.

Example: Let ''X'' be the blow-up of the complex projective plane <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> at a point ''p''. Let ''H'' be the pullback to ''X'' of a line on <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math>, and let ''E'' be the exceptional curve of the blow-up <math>\pi\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^2</math>. Then ''X'' has Picard number 2, meaning that the real vector space <math>N^1(X)</math> has dimension 2. By the geometry of convex cones of dimension 2, the nef cone must be spanned by two rays; explicitly, these are the rays spanned by ''H'' and ''H'' − ''E''.<ref>Kollár & Mori (1998), Lemma 1.22 and Example 1.23(1).</ref> In this example, both rays correspond to contractions of ''X'': ''H'' gives the birational morphism <math>X\to\mathbb{P}^2</math>, and ''H'' − ''E'' gives a fibration <math>X\to\mathbb{P}^1</math> with fibers isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> (corresponding to the lines in <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> through the point ''p''). Since the nef cone of ''X'' has no other nontrivial faces, these are the only nontrivial contractions of ''X''; that would be harder to see without the relation to convex cones.
